opus-5.5.text:
I think online resources played a really important role, especially in the early stages. When I was starting out, a lot of what I learned didn't come from a formal classroom. It came from reading things people had shared online: tutorials, forum discussions, problem sets, and later open source code. For someone who's curious but doesn't yet have a clear path, that kind of access matters a lot. You can just start trying things without anyone giving you permission.

One thing I appreciate about programming in particular is that the feedback loop is immediate. You write something, run it, and it either works or it doesn't. Online resources make that loop even richer, because when you get stuck you can find someone who hit the same problem before, read how they reasoned about it, and learn not just the answer but the way of thinking.

Later on, open source became the biggest resource for me. Reading real code written by strong engineers teaches you things a textbook can't, like how people structure systems, handle edge cases, and make trade-offs. And eventually you realize you can contribute back. That's part of why I care so much about building open source projects myself. Many people helped me learn just by putting their work out there, and I hope the things we build can do the same for the next person who's just getting started.

That said, I'd add one caveat. Resources are only half of it. The other half is having a problem you really want to solve. Online materials are most powerful when you're pulling knowledge toward a goal, not just passively consuming it. That's when the learning really sticks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, online programming resources were essential for me, and I think they're essential for most people entering computer science today.

When I was first getting into this, the formal path, the university courses, gave me foundations. But the things that really pulled me in were open source projects and the communities around them. You could read the actual code of a real system, see how people made design decisions, and ask questions on a mailing list or a GitHub issue and have someone far more experienced respond. That kind of access didn't exist a generation earlier. You had to be in the right lab or company to see how things were really built.

I'd point to a few specific ways these resources matter.

First, they lower the barrier to starting. You don't need permission. You can watch a lecture, read documentation, run a tutorial, and be writing code the same afternoon. For someone from a place without a strong local CS ecosystem, that's enormous.

Second, and I think this is underrated, they let you learn by contributing. When I worked on XGBoost and later on TVM and the MLC projects, a huge fraction of what I learned came from people filing issues, sending pull requests, and arguing with me about design. Open source turns learning into a two-way conversation. You're not just consuming a course, you're building something people depend on, and that feedback loop teaches you faster than any textbook.

Third, these resources compress the distance between research and practice. A paper comes out, and within weeks there's a reference implementation, a blog post explaining it, and a discussion thread where people try to reproduce it. That rapid cycle is how a student can go from reading about gradient boosting or compiler optimization to actually shipping a system.

I'll add one caution, though. There's so much material now that it's easy to stay in tutorial mode forever. My advice is always to pick a real problem, something slightly beyond your current ability, and let the online resources serve that project rather than the other way around. The resources are the map, but you still have to walk the terrain.

So for someone like me, online resources didn't just help me enter computer science. They shaped the kind of computer scientist I became, one who thinks of building in the open as the default.

r001.rationale: The response says online resources were essential and notes their value for people without a strong local CS ecosystem, but it does not state that Tianqi Chen’s county high school lacked introductory competition resources.

astra-6.text:
I think online programming resources make computer science much more accessible. You can start with a question, find a tutorial or an example, and then try something yourself. You don’t have to wait until you’ve taken a particular course to begin exploring.

For someone like me, that opportunity to learn by doing is really valuable. When you get stuck, you can see how other people approach a problem, ask questions, and build on what you’ve learned. The resources give you a starting point, but experimenting and making mistakes are what help you develop your understanding.
